about: Signals: announcements, commitments, gatherings and findings that show which way heat policy and practice are moving in South and Southeast Asia. A commitment climbs a ladder (announced, adopted, funded, delivered, evaluated) and each move is dated in its history; an announcement is a weak signal, and each rung is stronger evidence that change is real. Every signal reuses a source the site has already checked, or passed its own check (research/2026-11/signals-cop31/). The ladder records how far each signal has got, never how well an institution performs. Checked by build-data.js --check.

ladder.label: Announced
ladder.means: Said in public. A weak signal on its own: announcements happen whether or not anything follows.

ladder.label: Adopted
ladder.means: Made formal: a plan approved, a rule changed, an office set up.

ladder.label: Funded
ladder.means: Money committed to it, whether or not the amount is public.

ladder.label: Delivered
ladder.means: Something exists that people can use: a service open, a guide published, money paid out.

ladder.label: Evaluated
ladder.means: Its results were measured and published.

kinds.label: Commitment
kinds.means: Something an institution has promised or started; it climbs the ladder.

kinds.label: Gathering
kinds.means: A conference or forum where the field meets; what it produces may become commitments.

kinds.label: Finding
kinds.means: New science that changes how heat is understood.

kinds.label: Guidance
kinds.means: A framework or guide published for others to use.

groups.label: COP31 watch
groups.intro: What we are watching for heat at COP31. Each item is added only after its source passes the site's check, on the rung it has truly reached; almost everything at a conference starts as an announcement.

reading.label: A reading so far, after check-in 3 (18 November)
reading.text: COP31's heat story is running through cooling, health and money, while we have so far found little on heat itself in the negotiating texts. The cooling roadmap and WHO's El Niño plan sit outside the negotiated decisions. No heat commitment by India, Bangladesh, the Philippines or Thailand has been found in the coverage yet. This is a reading of what the watch has found, not a finding, and it will be revisited at the last check-in and when the conference closes.

signals.title: COP31 opens in Antalya
signals.summary: COP31, the UN climate conference, is held in Antalya from 9 to 20 November 2026.

signals.title: 2026 will be one of the four warmest years on record
signals.summary: WMO's State of the Climate Update 2026, released as COP31 opened, finds that the past 12 years have each been the warmest on record and the past four the top four. The global average surface temperature for January to September 2026 was about 1.47 °C above the pre-industrial average. In early November the EU's Copernicus service said 2026 is most likely to be the second-hottest year on record. It estimates that 146.5 million people in India were exposed to extreme heat in an April 2026 heatwave, and that the number of countries reporting multi-hazard early warning systems rose from 56 in 2015 to 136 in 2025.
signals.next: A finding, not a commitment: watch whether heat plans and budgets are sized for the heat these years now bring, not the heat people remember.

signals.title: El Niño set to bring more heat into 2027
signals.summary: By mid-August 2026 El Niño had become firmly established. WMO reports it has been intensifying since August and is expected to be the strongest on record by December, set to unleash even more heat and extreme weather well into 2027. WMO calls it a risk multiplier for health, and reports that WHO has, for the first time, classified the anticipated health impacts as a health emergency.
signals.next: Early warnings and heat plans ready for the 2027 hot season, above all in Southeast Asia, where El Niño and warming broke records in April 2016.

signals.title: Warming will overshoot 1.5 °C: the Emissions Gap Report 2026
signals.summary: UNEP's Emissions Gap Report 2026, The Point of Return, finds that with global temperature rise set to exceed 1.5 °C, urgent and stringent cuts are needed to minimise the size and length of the overshoot and return to 1.5 °C by the end of the century. If current policies continue, warming could reach 2.8 °C this century; if all national pledges are delivered, 2.6 °C.
signals.who: UNEP, with PBL Netherlands Environmental Assessment Agency
signals.next: A finding, not a commitment: watch whether adaptation plans for heat assume the warming these projections describe.

signals.title: The Antalya Initiative for Health Resilience (AIR) launches on Health Day
signals.summary: COP31 opened with the launch of the Antalya Initiative for Health Resilience (AIR), a voluntary platform for countries to share their experience of making health systems resilient to climate risks. Health Policy Watch calls it the Antalya Initiative for Resilient Health Systems; this page uses WHO's name. On the launch day no country had yet announced that it would take part. Alongside it, a joint initiative with WHO brings climate information into public health planning: a forecast of dangerously high temperatures, for example, can help hospitals prepare for more patients.

signals.title: The Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings opens for endorsement
signals.summary: Ahead of the conference, the COP31 Presidency launched the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, which aims for a 25% cut in the operational energy intensity of buildings worldwide by 2035, compared with 2020. Its actions include stronger energy codes, faster renovation and the electrification of heating and cooling. It covers buildings and energy as a whole, not heat alone; it bears on heat because cooler, more efficient buildings ease the indoor heat people live and work in, and the cost of cooling them.

signals.title: Only 35% of countries report health early warning systems for heat-related illness
signals.summary: IFRC's call to action for COP31 notes that only 35% of countries have reported having health early warning systems for heat-related illness. It asks for investment in multi-sector local action for cities and communities to reduce heat risk, from heat action plans and early warning to shock-responsive social protection and nature-based solutions.

signals.title: Adaptation finance covers a fraction of what is needed
signals.summary: UNEP's Adaptation Gap Report 2026 estimates that developing countries need about US$305 billion a year for adaptation by 2035. International public adaptation finance to developing countries was about US$28 to 32 billion in 2024. Even if the COP30 aim of tripling it is met, it would cover only about 20 to 29% of needs. The report covers adaptation as a whole, not heat alone; it bears on heat because heat plans draw on the same adaptation money.
signals.next: A finding, not a commitment: watch whether COP31's finance outcomes reach heat plans, and whether heat is named in them.

signals.title: India adds heatwaves to its notified natural calamities
signals.summary: In August 2026 India added heatwaves to its notified natural calamities, so national and state disaster response funds can pay for heatwave relief. Before, states could spend only up to 10% of their response fund on locally declared disasters such as heat. Heat mitigation projects are funded separately, from disaster mitigation funds.

signals.title: Singapore makes heat stress measures mandatory for outdoor work from 1 December 2026
signals.summary: The Ministry of Manpower announced on 28 August 2026 that enhanced heat stress measures, including drinking water, become mandatory for outdoor work from 1 December 2026, giving employers three months to prepare. Measures that had been recommended become requirements.

signals.title: Nearly all outdoor workers surveyed in Viet Nam's two largest cities report heat-related health problems
signals.summary: A 2026 study with UNDP surveyed 734 outdoor workers in Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City; 94% reported at least one heat-related health problem while working during heatwaves.

signals.next: A finding, not a commitment: watch whether Viet Nam's labour and social protection rules add heat, as the study suggests.

signals.title: World Bank: extreme heat already costs jobs and growth in South Asia's cities
signals.summary: The World Bank's report A Livable Future, published on 29 July 2026, finds extreme heat emerging as a major threat to jobs, productivity and growth across South Asia, and sets out how cities can protect them.
signals.next: A finding, not a commitment: watch whether city budgets in South Asia take up the report's measures.
